nodes.description: Progressive degeneration of the distal terminal sprouts of enlarged post-polio motor units produces ongoing muscle fiber denervation. Because overburdened surviving motor neurons can no longer fully compensate, denervation outpaces reinnervation, causing net loss of functioning motor units across spinal and bulbar myotomes. Electrophysiologically this manifests as increased jitter, blocking, increased fiber density, and spontaneous activity in newly weakened muscles.

nodes.description: During and after acute paralytic poliomyelitis, poliovirus-induced anterior horn cell loss leaves muscle fibers denervated. Surviving lower motor neurons reinnervate these orphaned fibers through terminal and collateral axonal sprouting at the neuromuscular junction, producing greatly enlarged motor units that can innervate up to seven times the normal number of muscle fibers. This compensatory reinnervation underlies functional recovery after acute polio but creates motor units far larger than physiological.
